I don't think I'm doing a good job communicating my view, so I will try to do better in this post. 

My view is shaped by over 15 years of writing about fashion (including the effects of fast fashion), reading @wdavidmarx's book "Status and Culture," and private conversations with technologist @quintendf. I will incorporate each of these influences as I make my argument. 

Let's put AI aside for now and talk about fashion, where I have better footing. We can start with a basic question: why were slim-fit pants considered good in the early 2000s, but bad today? The simple answer is because fashion moves through a lifecycle.

In the early 2000s, wearing slim-fit pants signaled that you were on the edge of culture. Perhaps you bucked gender norms, read Details Magazine, and drew inspiration from youthful European fashions. After all, this was a time when designers like Hedi Slimane and Raf Simons sent ectomorphic models marching down the runway in skin-tight clothes. And nands like The Strokes and The Libertines gave the style cultural relevance. 

Over time, the meaning of that look changed as it spread through the market. In the early 2000s, skin-tight pants looked cool because they signaled gender rebellion and rock-and-roll. But as it got mainstreamed through Mad Men and J. Crew, it became increasingly normalized and sanitized. Today, it represents the opposite of what it did in the early 2000s — gender conformity, out of touch, corporate drone. Also whatever Andrew Tate represents. 

This is the basic dynamic that drives fashion forward: people with low cultural capital copy people with high cultural capital, and then people with high cultural capital move on to distinguish themselves. This dynamic has been observed and remarked upon for hundreds of years, including by Bernard Mandeville (1714), Georg Simmel (1902), and Pierre Bourdieu (1979). 

This is why we're seeing a swing back towards baggier pants. People who put a lot of effort into improving their cultural capital don't want to look like everyday office drones, political interns, or Andrew Tate. 

Although, many astute fashion writers have remarked on a backlash to the backlash. Prada recently sent models back on the runway in slim-fit pants, probably because every male fashion influencer on Instagram nowadays is wearing the same look (e.g., cropped top, big pants, 70s hairstyle). 

Now let's look at the fast fashion industry. Fast fashion isn't bad just because the clothing is low quality. It's bad because it speeds up the trend cycle. In the distant past (say, pre-20th century), styles used to last at least a generation, if not more, because production was slow and information moved slowly across geography. Over the 20th century, as fashion went from bespoke to ready-to-wear, the production cycle sped up. By the end of the century, a look would still last maybe a decade before it got old. 

Today, developments in information technology and supply chain management have made it possible for a company to rip a look off the runway and put it into their stores before the original designer even has a chance to monetize their creation. So the criticism of companies like Shein, Zara, and H&M isn't just that they make crappy clothes (which they do), but that the minute you buy something, you realize the trend is already over. The people you tried to copy have already moved on, so you have to copy the next thing. Plus, as this copying process accelerates, designs can get more jumbled and ugly. Oh, double riders and fleece are trending? Let's make fleece double riders. It doesn't matter if it looks like ass — the thing won't stick around in the market long anyway. 

In his book Status and Culture, @wdavidmarx talks about how people's pursuit of status moves culture forward. Much of the book draws from varoius fields, such as sociology, anthropology, media studies, and the like. But then the last part of the book deals with something curious: Why can various fashions define previous decades, but things have not changed much since the 1990s? Indeed, I would argue that the last big innovation in menswear happened in the 1980s/ 90s with Japanese designers like Yohji Yamamoto and Issey Mikaye. Menswear has been backwards looking every since — never forward. 

Every era in the past had a distinct fashion. The 1960s had Mods and the Peacock Revolution, the 1970s had hippies and bohemian dress, the 1980s had power suits and the return of prep. Yet, if you watch a 1990s episode of Friends ... we kind of still dress the same. Yes, the silhouettes have changed a little, but the styles are mostly identical. 

Marx suggests this is because status games mostly play out online, where cool things can become uncool in a matter of hours. As a result, nothing really takes hold, so we get fleeting fads instead of era-defining trends. Think of what happens with memes. Something starts funny, and then a corporation's social account uses it to seem relevant. Then the meme is decidedly uncool. 

I once had a conversation with @quintendf about this. He suggested that we might be approaching a period where creative people seek to do things off the internet. Maybe that means returning to zines and cassette tapes that are passed around through a dub of a dub. Or maybe it's sensory experiences you can only have in person. During our conversation, I said that for this to happen, we need affordable housing in densely populated areas so creative people can interact with each other offline. And not feel pressured to maximize their income by selling themselves online. 

Which brings us back to AI. That Yung Lean video originally went viral because people found it moving. I remember reposting it on Twitter, which led several people to question whether I was secretly paid behind the scenes to do so (I wasn't, as I don't do paid tweets). To me, their questioning only underscores how natural that viral moment was—the video moved lots of people, so they shared it on their socials. 

Now that it has been endlessly copied in such trite, meaningless ways, the visual effect feels ever hollower. It has become a meme. As one person put it, "I now cringe when I see it." 

If we look back on history, we can see distinct creative movements in art, music, furniture design, fashion, architecture, and more. Neoclassicism led to Romanticism; Art Deco eventually led to mid-century modernism; big-band swing music led to bebop. These movements all follow a familiar formula: a zeitgeist led to a backlash, which created yet another zeitgeist. 

How can we have a creative zeitgeist when nothing is allowed to take hold? When every visual language is so easily replicated through AI tools and turned into memes? When visual language speeds from cool to cliché and then gets used by people with low cultural capital? 

This is what I meant when I said that AI may contribute to our cultural stagnation. The issue isn't whether AI detracts from the original work. Indeed, it can elevate the original artist and bring them more attention. The question is whether this is good for people who care about creative integrity for its own sake — outside of notions of monetary rewards or fame. And whether this is good for culture.

Generative language modeling for antibody CDR grafting and alignment-driven de novo design

1. The paper introduces GenCDR, a framework-first autoregressive (LLaMA-style) antibody language model: it reads all framework regions (FR1–FR4) as the prompt, then generates all CDRs jointly as a variable-length response, creating a clean prompt–response boundary for reward attribution and alignment.

2. This re-ordering directly targets the core de novo antibody problem as an infilling task: CDR design conditioned on a fixed scaffold. Unlike left-to-right decoding (where early CDRs lack downstream framework context), GenCDR generates CDRs with full framework context available from the start.

3. GenCDR is presented as a model family covering common design settings: IgGenCDR (unpaired human OAS, ~254M sequences), p-IgGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~1.8M natively paired VH–VL sequences), and NanoGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~6.5M camelid VHH from INDI plus human OAS heavy chains in a 1:1 mixture to preserve humanness on humanized scaffolds).

4. On CDR recovery (next-token prediction accuracy over CDR tokens) using a CDR3-disjoint held-out test set designed to reduce leakage, framework-first ordering improves over a same-sized left-to-right ablation and surpasses prior autoregressive baselines (including p-IgGen, ProGen2-OAS, and IgLM) across essentially all loops, with especially strong gains where downstream context matters most (e.g., CDR1).

5. De novo generation quality: when prompted with held-out frameworks and sampling CDRs jointly, GenCDR reproduces natural CDR length distributions closely (across all loops), while maintaining human-likeness (OASis), naturalness (ESM-2 PLL), and diversity/novelty with smooth trade-offs across sampling temperatures.

6. A key design consequence of the framework-first factorization is separable CDR likelihoods: GenCDR can score only the generated CDR block (rather than conflating framework+CDR likelihood), enabling clearer optimization targets and more principled alignment for CDR-centric objectives.

7. Likelihoods retain useful biological signal: GenCDR log-likelihood correlates zero-shot with experimental fitness/developability benchmarks (FLAb). The analysis also highlights assay locality: immunogenicity appears more CDR-driven, while expression is more framework-driven, and paired scoring (p-IgGenCDR) improves correlations when heavy+light are scored jointly.

8. NanoGenCDR extends the framework-first approach to nanobodies: fine-tuning closes the human→camelid distribution shift in CDR recovery, generates plausible/developable VHHs (including fold-confidence and developability flag rates comparable to reference), and improves humanness on humanized VHH scaffolds specifically due to the camelid+human mixture strategy.

9. Alignment-driven de novo design: the prompt–response boundary enables iterative alignment with weighted DPO (wDPO) using rewards computed only on the generated CDR completion. They optimize a composite reward from antibody–antigen co-folding metrics (Boltz-2) plus non-differentiable developability liability rules, demonstrating multi-objective steering without explicit antigen encoding in the model input.

10. In a PD-L1 nanobody design benchmark, four rounds of alignment drive near-perfect compliance with length/liability constraints after one round (acceptance ~23.8% → ~99.8–100%), and achieve in silico interface metrics competitive with a structure-conditioned diffusion pipeline (BoltzGen) at roughly half the sampling budget, while producing sequences that remain more “natural” under independent language-model scoring—suggesting KL-anchored alignment can push target-facing metrics without excessive distributional drift.

Train frontier models with reinforcement learning at scale!

Miles is an open-source framework for large-scale RL post-training across LLMs and VLMs.

At this scale, RL is not just about choosing an algorithm like GRPO or PPO. You also need fast rollouts, distributed training, weight synchronization, memory management, and a way to keep the training data aligned with what the model actually generated.

Miles brings those pieces together.

SGLang handles high-throughput rollouts, while Megatron-LM or FSDP2 handles training. Rollout and training can run asynchronously, so generation does not have to stop every time the model updates.

For long multi-turn or tool-using trajectories, Miles also preserves the exact token IDs produced during rollout before feeding them back into training. For MoE models, it can replay the expert-routing decisions from rollout during training to reduce mismatch between the two stages.

The system is built for very large models too.

In one reference setup, Miles runs asynchronous RL training for a 744B model across 64 GB300 GPUs. Its P2P weight synchronization also reduced the update time for a 1T-parameter Kimi-K2 setup from 53.3 seconds to 7.2 seconds.

Key capabilities:

• Fully asynchronous RL training
• SGLang rollouts with Megatron-LM or FSDP2 training
• GRPO, GSPO, PPO, REINFORCE++, SFT, and distillation
• Token-faithful training for multi-turn trajectories
• MoE routing replay between rollout and training
• CPU and NVMe optimizer-state offloading
• NVIDIA and AMD GPU support
• Agentic RL and sandboxed environments

It also extends beyond language models, with a separate Miles-Diffusion stack for RL post-training of diffusion models.

100% open source.
